title: Generalizing Abell-Tersoff bond-order potential with explicit high-order many-body correlations for robust extrapolation of potential energy surfaces
abstract: Machine-learning interatomic potentials enable accurate and efficient atomistic simulations, but their reliability for out-of-distribution configurations far beyond the training domain remains a significant challenge. Here, to tackle this challenge, we introduce a semiparametric interatomic potential based on a generalization of the Abell--Tersoff bond-order potential, with a chemically informed functional form and explicit high-order many-body correlations. The model is trained and evaluated on various datasets, including silicon, carbon, water, and small molecules, achieving interpolation accuracy comparable to that of existing MLIP models while demonstrating better extrapolation to unseen configurations, including those under high-pressure and high-temperature conditions. These results demonstrate that physically motivated constraints incorporated into the functional form can improve the extrapolation behavior of interatomic potentials, providing insights into the inductive biases that can be used to control extrapolation in machine-learning interatomic potentials.
summary: This paper introduces BOBOP, a generalized interatomic potential that merges the chemical intuition of the Abell-Tersoff model with explicit, high-order many-body correlations. It aims to overcome the critical weakness of standard MLIPs—poor extrapolation—by embedding physical constraints into the potential's functional form. The resulting model shows improved accuracy and transferability, particularly under extreme thermodynamic conditions.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is ensuring the reliability and physical accuracy of machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) when simulating atomic configurations far outside the training data distribution.
main_result: The proposed potential, BOBOP, successfully combines the chemically intuitive functional form of Abell-Tersoff potentials with explicit, high-order many-body correlations, leading to better extrapolation capabilities than standard MLIPs.
method: The authors generalize the Abell-Tersoff potential by constructing a semiparametric model that incorporates explicit three-, four-, and five-body descriptors derived from local atomic environments.
model_or_system: The model describes the potential energy surface (PES) of interacting atoms, using a modified Hamiltonian structure based on the Abell-Tersoff form. The local environment is encoded in a descriptor vector $\zeta_{ij}$ built from higher-order neighbor correlations.
key_observables: Potential Energy Surface (PES), bond order ($b_{ij}$), total energy ($E_{tot}$), and extrapolation accuracy under extreme conditions (high P/T).

paper_structure: The paper first establishes the limitations of existing potentials (Abell-Tersoff, standard MLIPs). It then introduces the BOBOP framework, detailing the construction of high-order descriptors ($\zeta_{ij}$) and the final energy functional. Finally, it discusses the theoretical implications of the effective body order and computational scaling.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter potentials, the methodology heavily relies on advanced machine learning descriptors and functional form constraints, making it relevant to the broader field of ML-physics and developing physically informed neural network potentials.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Two distinct bonding environments in planar CH4 that yield the same value of bond order bij in the Abell– Tersoff bond-order potential. The gray, red, blue, green, and yellow spheres represent atoms i, j, k, h, and u. Atom i is a carbon atom. Atoms j, k, h, and u are hydrogen atoms, which are indistinguishable under permutation. All bonds connected to atom i have the same length. The blue, red, purple, yellow, green, and cyan arcs indicate bond angles of 45◦, 45◦, 90◦, 135◦, 135◦, and 180◦, respectively.

FIG. 3. Asymptotic behavior of bond order bij for a nearest- neighbor bond in dimer, graphene, diamond, bc8, simple cu- bic, and fcc structures under isotropic scaling of the system. The bond-order profiles were averaged over four indepen- dently trained models, with the shaded regions indicating half of the standard deviation.

FIG. 2. Cohesive energy as a function of nearest-neighbor interatomic distances for (a) graphene, (b) diamond, (c) bc8, (d) simple cubic, and (e) fcc, calculated with BOBOP, DeePMD, and ACE trained on the limited-diversity carbon dataset. Each energy curve was averaged over four indepen- dently trained models, with the color-shaded regions indicat- ing the standard deviations. The gray-shaded regions indicate the per-atom energy range covered by the training dataset.

FIG. 4. Test RMSEs for energy as a function of the num- ber of training configurations of CH4. Results for BOBOP with explicit three- and four-body features are shown. Test RMSEs for three-body, four-body, and combined three- and four-body atom-centered descriptors with linear and neural- network outputs reported in Ref. [14] are also shown for com- parison. The left axis shows the RMSE normalized by the standard deviation of the energy over the CH4 dataset, while the right axis shows the corresponding RMSE in kcal/mol.

FIG. 5. An example of bond-energy degeneracy between two planar CH4 configurations. The bond energy Vij based on three-body features exhibits the same value for both config- urations, whereas that based on four-body features distin- guishes between them.
